## Methods

Protocol approval
The experimental procedures in this study were conducted in strict compliance with relevant ethical guidelines. The use of animals was reviewed and approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of South China University of Technology (Permit Number 2023088).

Materials
Sodium hyaluronate (HA-Na, Mw=4 kDa) was purchased from Bloomage Freda Biopharm (China). Dowex was purchased from sigma, tetrabutylammonium hydroxide di-tert-butyldicarbonate (Boc Anhydride), sodium chloride (NaCl), β-cyclodextrin (β-CD), 4-(t-Butyl)-phenylacetic acid, 4-dimethylaminopyridine (DMAP), 2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate, 2-hydroxypropyl methacrylate, N,N-dimethylacrylamide, phosphorus oxychloride, span 80, cyclohexane, N,N’-methylene diacrylamide, acrylic acid, and 3-Buten-1-amine hydrochloride were purchased from J&K Chemicals (China). (USA). PBS, Dulbecco’s modified Eagle medium, fetal bovine serum (FBS), penicillin/streptomycin, alpha-minimum essential medium (α-MEM), and L-glutamine were purchased from Gibco (USA). The Calcein-AM, propidium iodide, Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8), DAPI, TRIzol, Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP) Assay Kit, H&E staining kit, were purchased from Beyotime.

Synthesis of phosphorylated hydroxyethyl acrylate (Phos-HEA) and phosphorylated hydroxypropyl methacrylate (Phos-HPMA)
First, phosphorus oxychloride (7.46 g, 1.1 eq) was mixed with tetrahydrofuran (33 mL) and transferred into a 250 mL round-bottom flask under a nitrogen atmosphere. The flask was then placed in an ice bath for cooling. 2-hydroxyethyl acrylate (5.14 g, 1 eq) and triethylamine (4.93 g, 1.1 eq) were mixed with tetrahydrofuran (7 mL) and added into a dropping funnel under nitrogen. The solution was slowly dripped into the round-bottom flask. After 3 h of thorough reaction, 7.5 mL of water was added to the dropping funnel and slowly dripped into the flask to complete the hydrolysis. The reaction mixture was heated to room temperature and washed three times with saturated sodium chloride solution. The tetrahydrofuran (THF) was removed by rotary evaporation, yielding a light brown oily product (Phos-HEA). HPMA (6.38 g, 1 eq) was used to synthesize the Phos-HPMA following the same procedure.

Preparation of Phos-HEA microgel, DMAA microgel, and Phos-HPMA microgel
Phos-HEA (280 mg, 1 eq) was weighed and dissolved in 10 mL of H2O. Acrylic acid (10 μL, 0.1 eq) was added to the solution. N,N-dimethyl-bisacrylamide (MBA, 22 mg, 0.1 eq) was then dissolved in the solution, followed by the addition of a KPS solution (KPS (7 mg, 0.018 eq) dissolved in 100 μL of DI water). The reaction mixture was maintained under a nitrogen atmosphere at a stirring speed of 1200 rpm, and then mixed with 40 mL of cyclohexane and 900 μL of Span 80 to form a homogeneous emulsion. The emulsion was heated to 70 °C and stirred for 2 h. Afterward, the mixture was centrifuged, washed five times with anhydrous ethanol/DI water, and freeze-dried to obtain white Phos-HEA microgel. DMAA (142 mg, 1 eq) and Phos-HPMA (320 mg, 1 eq) were used to prepare the DMAA microgel and Phos-HPMA microgel, respectively, following the same procedure.

Preparation of Ac-Phos-HEA microgel, Ac-DMAA microgel, and Ac-Phos-HPMA microgel
Phos-HEA (1 g) was weighed and dispersed in 50 mL of H2O. Nitrogen gas was bubbled through the solution for 30 min to remove oxygen. EDC (3.68 g, 19.2 mmol) and NHS (552 mg, 4.8 mmol) were weighed and dissolved in the above solution to activate the carboxyl groups on the microgel surface. The solution was stirred for 2 h, after which 3-buteneamine hydrochloride (258 mg, 2.4 mmol) was added. The pH of the solution was adjusted to 8 using triethylamine. The reaction was carried out under a nitrogen atmosphere at room temperature for 12 h. The reaction mixture was placed in a 3500 Da dialysis bag and dialyzed for 5 days. Finally, the product was freeze-dried, yielding 75%. The DMAA microgel (1 g) and Phos-HPMA microgel (1 g) were used to prepare the Ac-DMAA microgel and Ac-Phos-HPMA microgel following the same procedure.

Synthesis of 4-(t-Butyl)-phenylacetic acid modified hyaluronic acid (HA-TP)
A solution of sodium hyaluronate (HA‑Na, 2.0 g) in deionized water was treated with Dowex resin (6.0 g) for ion exchange, then neutralized with tetra‑n‑butylammonium hydroxide (TBAOH) to obtain an aqueous HA‑TBA solution at pH 7.0. After freeze‑drying, the product was redissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO). HA‑TBA (1.0 g, 1.4 mmol in terms of disaccharide repeating units, 1 eq.), 4‑(tert‑butyl) phenylacetic acid (0.8 g, 4.2 mmol, 3 eq.), and 4‑dimethylaminopyridine (DMAP, 0.13 g, 1.05 mmol, 0.75 eq.) were dissolved in anhydrous DMSO (100 mL) at 25 °C. Under nitrogen atmosphere and at 25 °C, di‑tert‑butyldicarbonate (BOC₂O) was added dropwise. The mixture was warmed to 45 °C and stirred for 24 h. The resulting reaction mixture was dialyzed successively against DMSO, NaCl solution, and deionized water to remove low‑molecular‑weight impurities. Finally, the purified solution was freeze‑dried to afford the product as a white solid.

Synthesis of Ac-β-CD
Ac-β-CD was synthesized following established procedures from the literature33. In a typical preparation, β-cyclodextrin (β-CD, 10 g) was dissolved in dimethylformamide (DMF, 150 mL) and triethylamine (TEA, 7 mL). The solution was cooled to 0 °C with stirring. Acryloyl chloride (5 mL) was then introduced, and the reaction was allowed to proceed for 6 h. Following the reaction, the mixture was filtered to eliminate the precipitated trimethylamine hydrochloride salt. The filtrate was concentrated to roughly 20 mL via rotary evaporation. This concentrated solution was subsequently added dropwise into acetone (600 mL), which induced the formation of a white solid. The precipitate was collected, washed thoroughly with acetone, and finally subjected to freeze-drying to obtain the product.

Preparation of NC, NCLS, and CPAC hydrogel
For the NC hydrogel, HA-TP (1%), gelatin (3%), Ac-β-CD (5%), and Ac-Phos-HEA microgel (5%) were dissolved in PBS (900 μl). After complete dissolution, the solution was allowed to stand overnight. Subsequently, 100 μl of 0.5 wt% lithium phenyl-2,4,6-trimethylbenzoylphosphinate (LAP) was added, and polymerization was initiated under blue light (λ=405 nm, 350 mW/cm²) for 5 min to obtain the NC hydrogel. For the NCLS and CPAC hydrogels, the Ac-Phos-HEA microgels were replaced with an equal mass of Ac-DMAA microgels and Ac-Phos-HPMA microgels, respectively, while keeping all other conditions identical.

3D cell culture within hydrogels
The human mesenchymal stem cells (hMSCs) were purchased from REGEN-αGEEK Biotechnology Co. Ltd (a 65-year-old male donor). Primary hMSCs were cultured in αMEM supplemented with 16.7% FBS (Excel), 1% penicillin-streptomycin (Gibco), and 1% L-glutamine (Gibco), and passaged to passage 4 (P4) under conditions of 37 °C and 5% CO2. After 5 min of digestion with 0.05% trypsin (Gibco), the cells were collected. Following cell counting, the cells were placed into individual 1.5 mL Eppendorf tubes and centrifuged at 290 × g for 3 min, with the supernatant discarded. For each type of hydrogel, the encapsulation density of hMSCs was 1 × 10⁷ cells per mL of hydrogel precursor solution (NC, NCLS, or CPAC). After mixing, 50 µL of precursor solution containing hMSCs was crosslinked under blue light (λ=405 nm) for 5 min and transferred into a 24-well plate. Constructs were continuously cultured in either growth or osteogenic medium (10 mM β-glycerophosphate, 50 µg/mL ascorbic acid 2-phosphate, and 100 nM dexamethasone). For the EZH2 inhibitor group, the inhibitor (Cat: HY-148458, MCE) was added to osteogenic medium at a final concentration of 10 μM. Constructs were cultured in the inhibitor-containing osteogenic medium for 12 h, after which the medium was replaced with fresh osteogenic medium for continued culture.

Microgel shrinkage quantification
Microgel shrinkage was quantified by capturing images of Phos-HEA and Phos-HPMA microgels before and after ALP treatment using an inverted microscope. Fifteen microgels were randomly selected from each group, and their diameters were measured using NanoMeasure software (Version 1.2). The shrinkage of the microgels was quantified using NanoMeasure (Version 1.2) with quantitative analysis of fluorescence intensity conducted using ImageJ software (NIH).

Fabrication and rheological characterization of the NC and CPAC hydrogels
Rheological characterizations were performed using a TA Discovery HR-30 hybrid rheometer. Samples were formed in situ by pipetting a 50 µL monomer solution between the bottom HR-30 hybrid rheometer plate and an 8 mm flat plate, and the experiment was initiated after photopolymerization (λ=365 nm, 396 mW/cm2). Evolution experiments were performed at 37 °C. Time sweep measurements were conducted at 37 °C with a fixed strain of 1% and a frequency of 10 rad/s for 120 s. For the alternating strain steps hear test, the temperature was maintained at 37 °C, with a frequency of 10 rad/s. The strain was alternated between 60% (45 s) and 1% (45 s) for three full cycles to obtain the step shear profile. The stress relaxation properties of the samples were measured from compression tests of the gel discs (8 mm in diameter, 2 mm thick). The gel discs were compressed to 15% strain with a deformation rate of 0.3 mm s−1 and held for 300 s to obtain the stress relaxation curve. The Young’s modulus was then calculated as the slope of the linear region of the resulting stress‑strain curve. Each sample group was tested independently three times to ensure reproducibility.

Phos-HPMA microgel mediated the heterogeneous distribution of matrix stiffness in the CPAC Hydrogel
Nanoindentation technology was applied to characterize the Young’s modulus distribution of both hydrogels under underwater conditions via a Piuma nanoindenter (Optics 11, Netherlands). Specifically, the hydrogels were maintained in PBS at 37 °C for 1 h before being loaded onto the plate. We randomly selected a 350 × 350 μm square matrix area on the surface of the samples and performed nanoindentation measurements at intervals of 50 μm. A total of 8 × 8 valid Young’s modulus data points were obtained, forming a heatmap. The selected areas were random, and the measurements were repeated three times.

Real-time quantitative PCR
Total RNA was isolated from cultured samples using TRIZOL reagent (Vazyme, R401-01) following the manufacturer’s protocol. RNA concentration and purity were assessed by spectrophotometric measurement (NanoDrop 300, Thermo Fisher Scientific). First-strand cDNA synthesis was performed using PrimeScript RT Master Mix (Takara, RR014A) according to the manufacturer’s specifications. Quantitative PCR was carried out using TB Green Premix Ex Taq (Takara, RR820A) on a LightCycler 480 instrument (Roche Diagnostics). The thermal cycling protocol comprised: initial denaturation at 95 °C for 30 s, followed by 40 cycles of amplification (95 °C for 5 s, 60 °C for 30 s), and a final dissociation stage (95 °C for 15 s, 60 °C for 1 min, and 95 °C for 15 s). GAPDH served as the endogenous control for normalization. Relative gene expression levels were determined using the comparative 2−ΔΔCT method. Primer sequences are provided in Supplementary Table 1.

Immunofluorescence staining
Following a brief PBS rinse, specimens were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (Aname, #153799) for 30 min at ambient temperature. After two additional PBS washes, samples were permeabilized and blocked for 2 h at room temperature using PBS containing 3% bovine serum albumin (Millipore, #S30) and 0.25% Triton X-100 (Sigma, #T8787). Primary antibody incubation was carried out overnight at 4 °C in blocking buffer. Unbound antibodies were removed through three washes with dilution buffer, followed by 1-h incubation with Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated secondary antibody (1:200 dilution). For cytoskeletal and nuclear visualization, samples were subsequently treated with phalloidin (1:400, 1 h) and DAPI (1:100, 30 min). Fluorescence imaging was performed using a Zeiss LSM780 confocal system, with quantitative analysis of fluorescence intensity conducted using ImageJ software (NIH).
The primary antibodies used were as follows: anti-Col 1 (Cat. #14695-1-AP, ProteinTech, 1:500), anti-ALP (Cat. #DF6225, Affinity, 1:500), anti-FAK (phospho Y397) (Cat. # 66258-1-lg, ProteinTech, 1:500), anti-paxillin (Cat. # 10029-1-lg, ProteinTech, 1:500), anti-phospho-MYH9 (Ser1943) (Cat. # AF4425, Affinity, 1:500), anti- EZH2 (Cat. #21800-1-AP, ProteinTech, 1:500), anti-H3K27me3 (Cat. #A2363, Abclonal, 1:500).
The secondary antibodies used were as follows: CoraLite488-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (H+L) (Cat. #SA0013-1, ProteinTech, 1:500), CoraLite488-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG (H+L) (Cat. #SA0013-2, ProteinTech, 1:500), and goat anti-rabbit Alexa Fluor 594 (Cat. #S0006, Affinity, 1:500).

Western blot
Cellular proteins were lysed using ice-cold RIPA buffer containing 1 mM phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride. Nuclear and cytoplasmic fractions were isolated following the supplier’s protocol (Beyotime, Cat. #P0013B). Protein concentrations were determined using a bicinchoninic acid assay, followed by heat denaturation at 98 °C for 15 min. Protein samples (20 µg) were resolved on 10% SDS‒PAGE gels, initially at 80 V for 30 min and subsequently at 120 V for 80 min. Separated proteins were transferred onto PVDF membranes at 300 mA for 120 min. Membranes were blocked with 5% nonfat milk for 1 h at room temperature, followed by incubation with primary antibodies at 4 °C overnight. HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies were applied for 1 h at room temperature. Protein bands were detected using an enhanced chemiluminescence substrate (Epizyme, Cat. #SQ201) and imaged with a Bio-Rad system (Tanon, Shanghai, China). Band intensities were quantified using Image Lab software (Bio-Rad). A fixed rectangular selection tool was applied to each target band, and local background signals were subtracted to obtain net intensities. To normalize for loading differences, target protein signals were adjusted relative to internal controls (e.g., GAPDH) within the same lane. Triplicate experimental data were processed using GraphPad Prism 9.0 and expressed as mean ± SD. Statistical comparisons were performed via unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-test, with significance set at p<0.05.

Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) and ChIP-qPCR
Cells were fixed with 1% formaldehyde and subsequently quenched with glycine. After washing with PBS, the fixed samples were suspended in cell lysis buffer (5 mM PIPES-KCl, pH 8.0, 85 mM KCl, 0.5% NP40), and the collected nuclei were stored at −80 °C as nuclei pellets or nuclear lysates dissolved in nuclei lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 10 mM EDTA, 1% SDS). For H3K27me3 ChIP, lysates were thawed and sonicated with Sonifier (BRANSON) to obtain chromatin fragments of 300–1000 bp, and 10-fold-diluted with ChIP dilution buffer (16.7 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 1.2 mM EDTA, 0.01% SDS, 1.1% Triron 100×, 167 mM NaCl). After double-dilution with a sonication buffer (90 mM Hepes pH 7.9, 220 mM NaCl, 10 mM EDTA, 1% NP40, 0.2% sodium deoxycholate, 0.2% SDS), nuclei were homogenized with a Bioruptor (Toshodenki). After washing, a complex of nuclear proteins/DNAs and antibodies against H3K27me3 (Proteintech; 39157; 5 ug used) was retrieved with Protein A- and Protein G-Dynabeads (Life Technologies). After the cross-linking was reversed, chromatin fragments were treated with RNase A and proteinase K. DNA was purified with phenol-chloroform extraction or Ampure XP (Beckman Coulter). In the ChIP-qPCR analyses, the values from the immunoprecipitated samples were normalized to input DNA. Primer sequences are listed in Supplementary Table 2.

Ratskull defect repair model
All experimental procedures involving animals were conducted in accordance with protocols approved by the Animal Experimentation Ethics Committee of the South China University of Technology (AEC No. 2023088). Nine 8-week-old male Sprague-Dawley (SD) rats were acclimatized for 7 days under controlled conditions (24–26 °C, 70% humidity). The rats were randomly allocated into four groups (n=3 per group): (1) NC hydrogel, (2) CPAC hydrogel, (3) CPAC hydrogel without MSCs (Control), and (4) non-treated control (Blank). Following institutional guidelines, anesthesia was induced via intramuscular injection of a ketamine-xylazine mixture (0.2% ketamine, 0.1% xylazine in saline). Aseptic surgical exposure of the calvarium was performed, and two critical-size defects were created in the calvarium with a trephine drill. In each animal, the contralateral defect served as an internal control. Primary rMSCs were expanded to passage 3 (P3) prior to encapsulation in hydrogels. Both NC and CPAC hydrogels, each containing 5×106 cells, were preconditioned in osteogenic medium for 3 days before implantation into the calvarial defects. The surgical site was subsequently closed via suturing. Following an 8-week recovery period, the rats were euthanized for analysis. Skull specimens were initially subjected to micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) scanning, followed by decalcification in 10% ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA, pH 7.4) for 2 months in preparation for immunohistochemical evaluation.

Quantification of micro-CT
Micro-CT Scanning and Analysis: Upon euthanasia, rat calvarial bones were isolated and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde. Fixed samples were scanned using a Micro-CT system (Quantum GX2, Perkinelmer AG) under the following conditions: 70 kV for 140 ms with a resolution setting of 25 μm and 1024×1024 pixels. Three-dimensional reconstruction and subsequent data analysis of the defect region were performed to quantify bone regeneration. Key outcomes included bone volume (BV), bone volume/tissue volume (BV/TV), and bone surface/tissue volume (BS/TV).

Immunohistochemical staining
The skull specimens were first fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 48 h to ensure proper preservation of tissue morphology and antigens. Following fixation, the samples underwent mild decalcification with 10% EDTA solution (pH 7.4, 25 °C) for 6 weeks. Tissue dehydration was performed through a graded ethanol series (30–100%), with subsequent xylene clearing and paraffin embedding. Serial sections (4 μm thickness) were prepared for histological evaluation.
Tissue sections were subjected to H&E and Masson’s trichrome staining according to standard protocols, followed by coverslipping with mounting medium. For immunohistochemical detection, sections were incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies targeting osteocalcin (OCN; 1:100 dilution, DF12303, Affinity). Following primary antibody incubation, sections were treated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibody (room temperature, 30 min) and developed with diaminobenzidine substrate (10 min, room temperature). All stained sections were permanently mounted for microscopic evaluation.

Theoretical analysis of CPAC hydrogel deformation
Using elasticity theory, we analyzed how the hydrogel deforms in response to changes in the radius of the medium ball. Let the ball initially have radius R0, which then changes to R. Due to strong interactions at the interface, the surrounding hydrogel is perturbed accordingly. As a continuous elastic material, the hydrogel’s deformation can be described in spherical coordinates by the displacement components ur, uθ, uφ. Because of the spherical symmetry, only the radial displacement is nonzero, giving uθ=0 and uφ=0.
According to elasticity theory, the equilibrium is expressed as:
1 ∂ (r2Eu) = const (1)
r2 ∂r r
where E is the Young’s modulus. This system is subject to two boundary conditions: (1) At infinity (r→∞), the deformation vanishes, i.e., u→0; (2) At the ball’s surface (r=R0), the radial displacement equals the radius change, i.e., u=R-R0. Solving Eq. (1) under these conditions, we can obtain the expression for the radial displacement.
Generally, the Young’s modulus is assumed to be a fixed value (E=E0), then the solution of Eq. (1) yields:
u = (R-R0) R0^2 / r^2 (2)
The above equation shows that the hydrogel deforms radially around the ball, with greater deformation arising from larger radius changes.
For cases like the experiments conducted here, E is not fixed. When the hydrogel deforms, its local properties, such as polymer structures and interactions, change, which in turn alters E. The relationship between E and hydrogel deformation may be complex, but in the small deformation limit, we assume E is proportional to the deformation. Therefore, E can be approximated as a linear function, E=E0+kur, where E0 is the Young’s modulus of the undeformed hydrogel, and k is a constant that characterizes the dependence of E on ur. Solving Eq. (1) with this assumption yields:
E = 1/2 E0 + 1/2 sqrt(E0^2 + 4kbr^-2) (3)
where b=R0^2 k (R-R0)^2 + E0 (R-R0). Note that r≥R0 in the above equation. This expression shows that the Young’s modulus varies radially around the medium ball. As r decreases, E increases, meaning the Young’s modulus is greater closer to the ball’s surface. Equation (3) matches well with our experimental data, Supplementary Fig. 11a. By fitting the experimental data, we determine E0=270.26 Pa, and k= -21.26 Pa/μm or -2.13×10^7 N/m^3.
Solving Eq. (1) also provides the analytical solution for the radial displacement:
ur = -1/2k (E0 + sqrt(E0^2 + 4kbr^-2)) (4)
Equation (4) shows that the hydrogel deforms radially around the ball, with greater deformation arising from larger radius changes (Supplementary Fig. 11b).

Methods for ALP inhibitor use
ALP inhibitor (Beyotime, Cat# ST019) was prepared as a 10 mM stock solution using sterile 1× PBS. For experiments, the inhibitor was added to the culture medium at a final concentration of 0.1 mM and applied for 72 h. For the control group, an equal volume of PBS was added.

Methods for ALP activity quantification and the CCK-8 assay
The ALP activity in the culture medium was quantified using a commercial colorimetric assay kit (Beyotime, Cat# P0321S) based on the hydrolysis of p-nitrophenyl phosphate (pNPP). Specifically, after the designated treatments, the culture medium was collected and centrifuged to remove debris. Then, 50 µL of the supernatant was mixed with 50 µL of the pNPP substrate working solution in a 96-well plate and incubated in the dark at 37 °C for 30 min. The enzymatic reaction was terminated by adding the stop solution provided in the kit. The absorbance of the yellow reaction product, p-nitrophenol, was immediately measured at 405 nm using a microplate reader. A standard curve was established using p-nitrophenol standards, and the ALP activity was calculated for each sample based on the absorbance readings. All assays were performed in triplicate.
Cell viability was assessed using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8; Beyotime, Cat# C0038). Following the designated treatments, 100 µL of the CCK-8 reagent was directly added to each well (900 µL culture medium with one hydrogel). The plate was then incubated at 37 °C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO2 for 2 h. After incubation, the absorbance of each well was measured at a wavelength of 450 nm using a microplate reader. Wells containing culture medium and CCK-8 reagent without cells were used as blanks for background subtraction. Cell viability was calculated as a percentage relative to the untreated cells (set as 100%), using the following formula:
Viability (%) = (As - Ab) / (Ac - Ab) × 100% (5)
where As is the absorbance of the sample (treated cells), Ac is the absorbance of the control (untreated cells), and Ab is the absorbance of the blank. All experiments were performed with three independent replicates. Day 0 indicates the viability of MSCs before encapsulation, while day 3 represents the viability after MSCs were loaded in NC and CPAC hydrogels for 3 days.

Methods for ALP activity quantification
The alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity in the culture medium was quantified using a commercial colorimetric assay kit (Beyotime, cat# P0321S) based on the hydrolysis of p-nitrophenyl phosphate (pNPP). The specific procedure was as follows: After the designated treatments, the culture medium was collected and centrifuged. Then, 50 µL of the supernatant was mixed with 50 µL of the pNPP substrate working solution in a 96-well plate and incubated in the dark at 37 °C for 30 min. The enzymatic reaction was terminated by adding the stop solution provided in the kit. The absorbance of the yellow reaction product, p-nitrophenol, was immediately measured at 405 nm using a microplate reader. A standard curve was generated using p-nitrophenol standards, and the ALP activity was calculated for each sample based on the absorbance readings. All assays were performed in triplicate.

Methods for EdU incorporation assays and live/dead staining
The alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity in the culture medium was quantified using a commercial colorimetric assay kit (Beyotime, cat# P0321S) based on the hydrolysis of p-nitrophenyl phosphate (pNPP). The specific procedure was as follows: After the designated treatments, the culture medium was collected and centrifuged. Then, 50 µL of the supernatant was mixed with 50 µL of the pNPP substrate working solution in a 96-well plate and incubated in the dark at 37 °C for 30 min. The enzymatic reaction was terminated by adding the stop solution provided in the kit. The absorbance of the yellow reaction product, p-nitrophenol, was immediately measured at 405 nm using a microplate reader. A standard curve was generated using p-nitrophenol standards, and the ALP activity was calculated for each sample based on the absorbance readings. All assays were performed in triplicate.
For live/dead staining, a staining solution was prepared in 1× PBS containing Calcein-AM and propidium iodide (PI), each at a final concentration of 1 µM. The hydrogels cultured for 3 days in a 24‑well plate were carefully removed and transferred to a new plate, and 1 mL of the prepared staining solution was added to each well. The plate was then incubated at 37 °C in the dark for 30 min. Following incubation, the hydrogels were washed three times with 1× PBS. Finally, imaging was performed using a confocal laser scanning microscope with detection channels set to 488 nm and 594 nm.

Methods for in vivo implantation model and sample processing for ALP, nanoindentation and mass quantification
According to the previously described method for creating critical-size bone defects in rat calvaria, hydrogels loaded with rMSCs were implanted into the calvarial defect areas. The implanted hydrogels were retrieved at different time points: before implantation (0 h), and at 24 h and 72 h after implantation. The retrieved hydrogels were added to 1 mL of 1× PBS, thoroughly homogenized using a tissue grinder, and then centrifuged. The alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity in the hydrogel was quantified using a commercial colorimetric assay kit (Beyotime, cat# P0321S) based on the hydrolysis of p-nitrophenyl phosphate (pNPP). The specific procedure was as follows: 50 µL of the supernatant was mixed with 50 µL of the pNPP substrate working solution in a 96-well plate and incubated in the dark at 37 °C for 30 min. The enzymatic reaction was terminated by adding the stop solution provided in the kit. The absorbance of the yellow reaction product, p-nitrophenol, was immediately measured at 405 nm using a microplate reader. A standard curve was generated using p-nitrophenol standards, and the ALP activity was calculated for each sample based on the absorbance readings. All assays were performed in triplicate.
For nanoindentation testing, the extracted hydrogels were fixed onto glass slides. An 8×8 matrix of points, with each point spaced 50 μm apart, was randomly selected on the hydrogel surface. The effective Young’s modulus at each point in the matrix was measured using a nanoindenter.
For the degradation experiment, the implanted hydrogels were retrieved at different time points, freeze-dried, and weighed (recorded as Wx). Taking the mass of the freeze-dried hydrogel sample before implantation as W0, the degradation rate of the hydrogel was calculated as follows:
D = Wx / W0 × 100% (6)
All samples in each group were tested in three independent experiments to ensure reproducibility.

Method for alkaline phosphatase color development kit
After fixation with paraformaldehyde, the hydrogel was cryosectioned into 8 μm thin slices. The resulting slices were washed three times with PBS. A working solution was prepared according to the manufacturer’s instructions of the BCIP/NBT Alkaline Phosphatase Color Development Kit (Beyotime, cat# C3206). The sections were fully covered with the working solution and incubated at room temperature in the dark for 30 min. The color development reaction was terminated by washing twice, and images were captured using an inverted microscope.

Statistics and reproducibility
Experiments included triplicate samples (n=3), and results are shown as mean ± standard deviation. Statistical significance was determined using GraphPad Prism (version 9.0.0) and Origin (version 2018). Comparisons between two groups were analyzed by an independent t-test, while comparisons across more than two groups were analyzed by one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple comparison test. In all analyses, statistical significance was defined as p<0.05.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

This study presents a novel hydrogel material—cell-programmed adaptive contraction (CPAC) hydrogel—that can respond to alkaline phosphatase (ALP) signals secreted by cells, leading to contraction of the embedded microgels within the hydrogel and resulting in local stiffness enhancement, ultimately forming a heterogeneous hydrogel structure. While the CPAC hydrogel demonstrates innovative bio-responsiveness and potential for bone repair, there are several shortcomings and potential gaps in the study. Therefore, we do not recommend the article for publication in Nat. Commun. at this stage.
1.The design of the CPAC hydrogel relies solely on ALP as the key enzymatic marker for regulation. However, it remains unclear whether other enzymes within the phosphatase family could also influence this process, potentially leading to non-specific reactions. Additionally, the dynamics of ALP release during MSC osteogenic differentiation are not well defined.
2.The CPAC hydrogel mimics the mechanical heterogeneity of natural ECM through the contraction of microgels and local stiffness enhancement. However, whether the hydrogel can achieve precise and controllable gradient variations in local stiffness remains a concern. In the complex in vivo biological environment, the hydrogel may be influenced by external factors such as temperature and pH, leading to unpredictable fluctuations in its mechanical properties. This could affect the cells' response to the material, particularly if the local stiffness of the hydrogel becomes uneven, potentially causing misalignment in stem cell differentiation.
3.In this study, the CPAC hydrogel responds to ALP and alters its structure within a short period of time, but its stability in vivo or in vivo or in vivo or in vivo or in long-term experiments has not been sufficiently validated.
4.Although the hydrogel promotes MSC osteogenic differentiation, the effects on cell proliferation and survival have not been adequately explored. The contraction of the microgels may lead to changes in the intercellular space, further affecting cell expansion and proliferation. If the hydrogel does not provide sufficient support or space during differentiation, it may limit the functional repair of the cells.
5.The authors indicate that the expression levels of miR-124, miR-214, and miR-26a are elevated in the CPAC hydrogel group, and this is significantly correlated with a decrease in the expression of EZH2 and its downstream target H3K27me3. However, the lack of validation through anti-miR treatment raises concerns about the reliability of this correlation.
6.In Figure 5g, the immunofluorescence images for the control group are not shown.
7.In Figures 3b, 3c, and 5c, g, a significant proportion of suspected overexposed areas can be observed. This raises concerns about the accuracy of the semi-quantitative analysis based on fluorescence intensity.
8.The regulatory effect of H3K27me3 on osteogenic-related genes has not been validated through relevant experiments.
9.In the in vivo experiments, only data from 8 weeks after hydrogel implantation are provided. This duration does not adequately reflect the effects of local network stiffening in promoting MSC osteogenic differentiation.
10.The size changes of CPAC hydrogel in a 1 U/mL ALP solution have been studied; however, the ALP concentration during in vivo or bone injury healing is unknown, and it remains unclear whether it would be sufficient to trigger the hydrogel's adaptive remodeling. Additionally, the hydrogel's contraction under in vivo conditions has not been characterized.

### Reviewer 2

The authors present a study focused on the development of a hydrogel system that mimics the dynamically evolving and heterogeneous extracellular matrix (ECM) environment during tissue development. Specifically, they engineer a cell-programmed adaptive contraction (CPAC) hydrogel containing ALP-responsive microgels that contract in response to alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity. This induces overall hydrogel network contraction and local matrix stiffening, thereby promoting osteogenic differentiation of mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs). The authors provide and test a hypothesis for the underlying mechanotransduction mechanism including upregulation of microRNA and demonstrate the translational potential of their system in a rat critical-size bone defect model, where they observed enhanced bone formation.
The study presents a dynamic hydrogel platform that responds to cell-released enzymes and modulates stem cell fate through dynamically changing the mechanical signals. The concept is interesting, and the authors have sought to perform both mechanistic investigation and in vivo validation. While the results are promising, additional experiments are required to support their main claims such as ‘‘ALP-induced gel contraction’’, ‘‘local stiffening’’ and ‘‘mechanical heterogeneity’’. Moreover, several aspects of the study require clarification, statistical information or further detail to strengthen its overall scientific rigor, reproducibility and impact.
Major comments:
• Novelty and significance: It would be helpful if the authors can explain more why this work is novel and their findings are significant for a broad impact.
• Study design: While this study probed an interesting concept, their main claims seem to have several gaps, across materials, in vitro- and in vivo models.
o From the materials aspect, the reliability relies on a thorough characterization of the mechanical properties and heterogeneity of their biomaterials.
o The range of mechanical stiffness such as magnitude, anisotropy seems unclear.
o From the cell biology perspective, whether the readouts are solely due to ALP, and cell-secreted ALP, or not, may require more rigorous investigation by setting up controls and perturbation experiments. It is known that cells also secrete other factors that block ALP acitivity.
o From the in vivo aspect, the complexity further increases in terms of proteins and cells in involved. The authors are recommended to add control experiments to demonstrate the enhanced bone formation is not by the gels along, nor other matrix factors, but exactly by their claimed mechanism.
• Abstract clarity: The abstract does not clearly convey how the hydrogel system works. Key elements, such as the main components of the hydrogel as well as the control groups used in the study, are not mentioned but are critical for interpreting the results.
• Introduction:
o The introduction would benefit from a comparison to naturally derived hydrogels such as collagen. How does the contractile behaviour of the presented system compare, and what advantages does it offer over existing ECM-mimetic materials?
o The exact composition of the hydrogel remains unclear in the introduction and Figure 1. Including a schematic that clearly explains the composition and assembly of the hydrogel from microgels and other components for all experimental hydrogel groups would greatly improve clarity. Also pay attention to complete & matching legends for the schematics.
• Figure 2g: It would be helpful to include confocal images of the hydrogels prior to ALP treatment to demonstrate the changes induced by contraction.
• Figure 2h: Please indicate which statistical test was used and annotate significance levels directly on the graph.
• You claim that “CPAC hydrogel can better facilitate stellate spreading”. Please explain where this can be seen or provide more morphological data to support it.
• Figures 3b/c: The CPAC hydrogels appear to have a higher cell density compared to NC controls. Is this a localized effect due to contraction, or does the material promote proliferation? Higher local cell density itself may influence osteogenic differentiation.
Related to this, can you comment on the macroscopic effect of ALP-mediated contraction on the entire hydrogel, does the hydrogel size change?
• Can you specify how the “high-modulus N,N-dimethylacrylamide (DMAA) microgels” compare to the previous control microgels (Phos-HEA) in terms of mechanical properties?
• The claim “NCLS hydrogels showed elevated osteogenic marker expression relative to NC hydrogels” is not evident from the data shown, please justify or explain more.
• Figure 4: Please provide rationale for the selection of mechanotransduction markers (pFAK, pMyosin IIa, Paxillin).

## Round 1 — Authors' Response

Thank you for this insightful and constructive comments. Regarding the specificity toward ALP, we do agree that other phosphatases (e.g., acid phosphatases) could potentially lead to the cleave of phosphate groups in our systems. Our design focused on ALP because of its well-established role as an early and strongly upregulated marker of osteogenic differentiation. Therefore, to test whether other phosphatases could also influence this system, we performed two control experiments: (i) CPAC hydrogels treated with ALP and an ALP inhibitor did not develop heterogeneous structures, and their storage modulus remained unchanged (Figure S12a, c), highlighting the dominant role of ALP in this heterogenization process. (ii) CPAC hydrogels treated with acid phosphatase (ACP) also failed to induce localized stiffening (Figure S12b), likely due to its limited activity under the neutral buffered conditions used. These results confirm that ALP is the primary enzyme driving the contraction-induced stiffening process in CPAC hydrogels.
Moreover, to validate the dynamics of ALP release during MSC differentiation, we quantified ALP levels in CPAC and NC hydrogels over 0–168 hours (Figure S12d). Both groups showed a gradual increase in ALP during culture, but the levels in CPAC hydrogels rose more steeply, reaching ~10 U/mL at 168 h, compared to ~5 U/mL in NC hydrogels. This sustained elevation indicates that CPAC hydrogels not only permit ALP secretion but also amplify it through the feedback between microgel contraction, local stiffening, and osteogenic activation.

Author Response:
We thank the reviewer for raising these important concerns regarding the precise control over local stiffness gradients and the influence of external factors like temperature and pH in the complex in vivo environment. Below, we address both of these aspects based on additional experiments:
1) Precise and controllable gradient variations in local stiffness:
We agree that achieving precise and controllable gradients in local stiffness is a key consideration for biomimetic materials. In our current design, the mechanical heterogeneity is dynamically evolved through a cell-driven feedback mechanism, rather than being pre-programmed with static, absolute precision. The contraction of microgels and local stiffness enhancement are primarily triggered by ALP secreted by MSCs themselves during early osteogenic differentiation, leading to self-regulated structural heterogeneity. This design more accurately mimics the dynamic and reciprocal cell-matrix interactions found in natural ECM, where the matrix evolves in response to cellular activity. To characterize this dynamic process and assess its controllability, we performed the following analyses:
i) Microscopic mechanical mapping: Nanoindentation mapping (Figure S16a) indicates that, while a degree of heterogeneity is present, as intended to mimic natural ECM, the stiffness variation occurs relatively uniformly without large, unpredictable fluctuations that would lead to detrimental misalignment in stem cell differentiation. This suggests that the cell-instructed heterogeneity may be more physiologically relevant than a perfectly engineered but static gradient.
ii) Macroscopic rheological analysis: Bulk storage modulus (G’) of the hydrogel was monitored over time during osteogenic differentiation. The data (Figure S16b) shows a consistent increase in overall stiffness, confirming that the CPAC hydrogel undergoes predictable and controlled temporal stiffening in response to cellular activity.

2) Potential influence of in vivo factors and hydrogel stability:
Regarding the potential effects of temperature and pH fluctuations in the in vivo environment, we conducted stability tests to assess the hydrogel’s response to changes in these parameters. The CPAC hydrogels were incubated in buffers with pH ranging from 7.2 to 7.8 and at different temperatures from 33 to 39 °C. The hydrogels maintained their structural integrity within the physiological range of pH (7.2-7.8) and temperature (33- 39 °C), showing no significant degradation in mechanical properties or unpredictable fluctuations in stiffness (Figure S16c-f). While the enzymatic activity of ALP can be modulated by environmental pH and temperature, our results indicate that slight variations within physiological ranges do not induce measurable changes in the hydrogel’s structure or its ability to remodel over a relatively long culture period. Methylation of H3K27 serves as a critical epigenetic switch determining the lineage commitment of MSCs, with elevated H3K27me3 levels on osteogenic gene promoters reported to suppress osteogenic differentiation by silencing key transcription factors such as RUNX2 [2-7]. To directly validate this regulatory mechanism in our system, we performed a ChIP-qPCR assay targeting the RUNX2 promoter. The results showed that H3K27me3 was enriched specifically at the upstream promoter region of RUNX2 rather than at unrelated genomic regions (Figure R1a). In MSCs cultured within CPAC hydrogels, both immunofluorescence and Western blot analyses confirmed a significant decrease in global H3K27me3 levels (Figures R1b and R1c), while RT-qPCR demonstrated a marked upregulation of RUNX2 transcription (Figure R1d). In summary, these findings demonstrate that H3K27me3 directly represses RUNX2 transcription, thereby limiting osteogenic differentiation, and that the CPAC hydrogel microenvironment alleviates this repression to promote osteogenesis.

SI materials and methods:
Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) and ChIP-qPCR
Cells were fixed with 1% formaldehyde and subsequently quenched with glycine. After washing with PBS, the fixed samples were suspended in cell lysis buffer (5 mM PIPES-KCl pH 8.0, 85 mM KCl, 0.5% NP40), and collected nuclei were stored at −80 °C as nuclear pellets or nuclear lysates dissolved in nuclei lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH8.0, 10 mM EDTA, 1% SDS). For H3K27me3 ChIP, lysates were thawed and sonicated with Sonifier (BRANSON) to obtain chromatin fragments of 300–1,000 bp, and 10-fold-diluted with ChIP dilution buffer (16.7 mM Tris-HCl pH8.0, 1.2 mM EDTA, 0.01% SDS, 1.1% Triron100×, 167 mM NaCl). After double-dilution with a sonication buffer (90 mM Hepes pH 7.9, 220 mM NaCl, 10 mM EDTA, 1% NP 40, 0.2% sodium deoxycholate, 0.2% SDS), nuclei were homogenized with a Bioruptor (Tosho denki). After washing, a complex of nuclear proteins/DNAs and antibodies against H3K27me3 (Proteintech; 39157; 5ug used) was retrieved with Protein A- and Protein G-Dynabeads (Life Technologies). After the cross-linking was reversed, chromatin fragments were treated with RNase A and proteinase K. DNA was purified with phenol-chloroform extraction or Ampure XP (Beckman Coulter).
In the ChIP-qPCR analyses, the values from the immunoprecipitated samples were normalized to input DNA. Primer sequences are listed in Table S2, Supporting Information.

Reviewer #2:
The authors present a study focused on the development of a hydrogel system that mimics the dynamically evolving and heterogeneous extracellular matrix (ECM) environment during tissue development. Specifically, they engineer a cell-programmed adaptive contraction (CPAC) hydrogel containing ALP-responsive microgels that contract in response to alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity. This induces overall hydrogel network contraction and local matrix stiffening, thereby promoting osteogenic differentiation of mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs). The authors provide and test a hypothesis for the underlying mechanotransduction mechanism including upregulation of microRNA and demonstrate the translational potential of their system in a rat critical-size bone defect model, where they observed enhanced bone formation.
The study presents a dynamic hydrogel platform that responds to cell-released enzymes and modulates stem cell fate through dynamically changing the mechanical signals. The concept is interesting, and the authors have sought to perform both mechanistic investigation and in vivo validation. While the results are promising, additional experiments are required to support their main claims such as ‘‘ALP-induced gel contraction’’, ‘‘local stiffening’’ and ‘‘mechanical heterogeneity’’. Moreover, several aspects of the study require clarification, statistical information or further detail to strengthen its overall scientific rigor, reproducibility and impact.
Major comments:
1. Novelty and significance: It would be helpful if the authors can explain more why this work is novel and their findings are significant for a broad impact.
Author Response:
We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. Previous biomaterials designed to mimic the ECM were predominantly based on preset static mechanical properties (e.g., uniform stiffness). While they could promote stem cell differentiation through mechanotransduction pathways (e.g., YAP/TAZ), they failed to replicate the spatiotemporally dynamic mechanical heterogeneity of natural ECM during development. The innovations and broad applicability of the CPAC hydrogel system proposed in this study are demonstrated in the following aspects:
1) Cell-driven dynamic remodeling: Our CPAC hydrogel leverages stem cell-secreted ALP to induce a hydrophilic-to-hydrophobic transition and local microgel contraction. This results in progressive, cell-programmed heterogenization of the network, closely resembling native bone ECM remodeling during development. This dynamic remodeling overcomes the spatiotemporal resolution limitations of existing photo- or enzyme-crosslinking methods by synchronizing material stiffening with stem cell differentiation.
2) Positive feedback regulation: The ALP-triggered local stiffening further amplifies ALP secretion, forming a closed-loop cycle of “mechanical signal-ALP release-hydrogel stiffening- amplified mechanical signal”. This reciprocal interaction better emulates the bidirectional crosstalk between developing ECM and cells, in contrast to the unidirectional mechanical cues of previous systems.
3) Spatiotemporally coordinated microenvironment: By enabling MSCs to construct a heterogeneous and adaptive microenvironment, the CPAC hydrogel supports bone-like ECM evolution. Its successful application in repairing critical-sized cranial defects in rats, with performance superior to conventional homogeneous hydrogels, highlighting its potential in clinical translation and the regeneration of other complex tissues.
4) Potential for personalized therapy: Since the remodeling process is driven by endogenous ALP secreted by the patient-derived stem cells, the CPAC system may reduce the need for exogenous growth factors, minimize immunological risks, and adapt to individual variations.
5) Paradigm shift in biomaterial design: This work shifts the focus from “static ECM mimicry” toward “dynamic cell-material interactions”, establishing a new design principle where cells instruct materials, and materials feedback to cells.

Author Response:
We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. To address these concerns, we performed additional characterizations of the CPAC hydrogel:
(i) Stiffness range: The Young’s modulus of CPAC hydrogels increased from ~3 kPa at day 0 to ~11 kPa after 3 days of MSC culture both in vitro and in vivo. This stiffening is driven by cell-mediated microgel contraction, confirming the autonomous remodeling capacity of the material.
(ii) Anisotropy: Compression tests were carried out in both parallel and perpendicular directions. The resulting stress-strain curves and moduli were consistent, indicating that CPAC hydrogels are mechanically isotropic at the bulk level.
(iii) Heterogeneity: Nanoindentation mapping revealed marked internal heterogeneity in both parallel and perpendicular directions. Local effective moduli ranged from ~0.5 kPa in softer regions to ~14 kPa in stiffer regions, demonstrating the dynamic formation of a heterogeneous microenvironment both in vitro and in vivo.
Together, these results provide a more complete mechanical characterization of CPAC hydrogels, confirming their ability to dynamically span a physiologically relevant stiffness range while maintaining isotropic bulk mechanics and pronounced local heterogeneity.

3. From the cell biology perspective, whether the readouts are solely due to ALP, and cell-secreted ALP, or not, may require more rigorous investigation by setting up controls and perturbation experiments. It is known that cells also secrete other factors that block ALP acitivity.
Author Response:
We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful comment. We agree that it is essential to rigorously evaluate whether ALP, particularly cell-secreted ALP, is the principal driver of CPAC hydrogel remodeling.
To this end, CPAC hydrogels were first cultured in PBS supplemented with ALP/ALP inhibitor. As shown in Figure S12a and S12c, inhibition of ALP abolished the formation of heterogeneous structures and prevented changes in storage modulus, confirming that ALP activity is required for CPAC remodeling.
To probe potential contributions from other phosphatases, CPAC hydrogels were treated with acid phosphatase. No appreciable heterogeneous structures were observed (Figure S12b), likely because acid phosphatase exhibits limited activity in the neutral PBS environment. Together with the fact that such phosphatases are secreted at low levels and primarily localized intracellularly, this suggests minimal impact on CPAC remodeling.
To address the possibility that MSCs secrete molecules capable of suppressing ALP activity, we measured ALP activity in the culture medium over time. The results showed a steady increase in ALP activity from 0 to 168 hours, indicating that any inhibitory factors are insufficient to block ALP function in this context.
Collectively, these results demonstrate that MSC-secreted ALP is the dominant factor driving microgel contraction and heterogeneous structure formation in CPAC hydrogels.

6. The introduction would benefit from a comparison to naturally derived hydrogels such as collagen. How does the contractile behaviour of the presented system compare, and what advantages does it offer over existing ECM-mimetic materials?
Author Response:
We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. Traditional collagen hydrogels typically exhibit a relatively homogeneous network structure with limited dynamic responsiveness, where remodeling relies on slow enzymatic degradation to facilitate cell migration and mineralization. Their static modulus and sluggish remodeling prevent them from rapidly adapting to the evolving mechanical needs of differentiating cells. In contrast, the CPAC hydrogel features a host-guest crosslinked network that provides significantly greater dynamic properties, better supporting such cellular processes. More importantly, its remodeling is actively programmed by the cells themselves, i.e., ALP secreted by cells triggers a hydrophilic-to-hydrophobic transition in the integrated microgels, driving localized contraction and heterogeneous stiffening that mimic the spatiotemporal heterogeneity of bone ECM during development. Furthermore, this cell-triggered contraction further amplifies mechanical signals, creating a self-reinforcing positive feedback loop. Therefore, CPAC hydrogels overcome the passive, slow-responding nature of collagen and other naturally derived ECM mimetics, offering a more precise and timely regulation of stem cell differentiation.

As shown in the Figure S17, MSCs in CPAC hydrogels exhibited significantly higher proliferation efficiency compared to those in NC hydrogels, while cell viability remained consistently high in both groups. Author Response:
We thank the reviewer for the comments. The selection of pFAK, pMyosin IIa, and Paxillin was based on their central and complementary roles in the focal adhesion-mediated mechanotransduction cascade. Specifically: 1) pFAK acts as the primary mecanosensor and signal amplifier, with its phosphorylation serving as an early indicator of force detection and conversion into biochemical signals; 2) pMyosin IIa functions as the intracellular force generator, reflecting the level of cell contractility and tension in response to the matrix; 3) Paxillin functions as a critical scaffolding protein, with its phosphorylation status reflecting the maturation, size, and stability of the focal adhesions necessary to effective force transmission. Monitoring these three markers together therefore provides an integrated readout of mechanotransduction, spanning force sensing, contractility, and adhesion reinforcement.

16. Figure 4b: Collagen I appears to be predominantly intracellular. Is there an explanation for this observation?
Author Response:
We greatly appreciate your insightful question. As a key marker of osteogenesis, type I collagen (Col1) is initially synthesized intracellularly as procollagen before being secreted and deposited into the ECM. At this early time point (3 days), MSCs have not yet deposited substantial extracellular collagen, which explains the predominantly intracellular signal. In addition, the multiple washing and permeabilization steps required for immunofluorescence staining may partially remove deposited extracellular Col1, and any remaining matrix-associated collagen may display fluorescence intensity too weak to be distinguished from the stronger intracellular signal.
To address this concern, we complemented our IF analysis with Masson’s trichrome staining on hydrogel cryosections. The darker blue areas observed in the CPAC group confirmed enhanced extracellular Col 1 deposition, supporting the conclusion that CPAC hydrogels promote osteogenic differentiation of MSCs.

17. The hydrogel is described as responsive to ALP secreted by MSCs, yet the immunofluorescence images show primarily intracellular ALP. Please clarify how this observation aligns with the proposed mechanism of hydrogel contraction, which relies on extracellular ALP activity.
Author Response:
We thank the reviewer for this insightful question. ALP is predominantly localized on the plasma membrane (via GPI anchors) as well as in intracellular compartments such as endoplasmic reticulum, and Golgi apparatus. Importantly, membrane-associated ALP can be released into the extracellular space by cleavage of its GPI anchor through specific enzyme, allowing it to diffuse into the hydrogel and trigger microgel contraction.
During the immunofluorescence staining process, the hydrogel undergoes sequential fixation, permeabilization, and multiple washing steps likely removed soluble or weakly bound ALP within the hydrogel matrix. Any residual extracellular ALP may also have been too faint to distinguish from the much stronger intracellular signal, explaining why the IF images appear to show primarily intracellular ALP.
To overcome this limitation, we additionally performed staining of hydrogel cryosections using a BCIP/NBT alkaline phosphatase color development kit. This assay confirmed the presence of extracellular ALP within the CPAC hydrogel matrix, with more intense staining compared to controls, supporting the conclusion that secreted ALP actively contributes to hydrogel remodeling.

26. You write that your skull specimens were decalcified for 2 months before fixation, whereas fixation is generally performed before decalcification to preserve tissue, cell and protein integrity. Could you please explain your choice of procedure and whether that could affect the staining results?
Author Response:
We thank the reviewer for this important comment. We apologize for the ambiguity in our original description. In our experiments, the skull specimens were first fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 48 hours to ensure proper preservation of tissue morphology and antigens. Following fixation, the samples underwent mild decalcification with 10% EDTA solution (pH 7.4, 25 °C) for 6 weeks. Compared with rapid decalcification agents, this method maximally preserves antigen activity and is widely regarded as the gold standard for immunohistochemistry (IHC). Finally, standard antigen retrieval using citrate buffer was performed on paraffin-embedded tissue sections to unmask epitopes prior to IHC staining. Our approach is consistent with established protocols reported in classical literature [8,9]. Therefore, fixation was indeed performed before decalcification, and the chosen method ensures reliable antigen preservation without compromising the IHC results.
The corresponding paragraphs in SI now reads:
Immunohistochemical staining
Following decalcification, specimens were fixed in 4% formaldehyde for 24 hours, followed by extensive washing with deionized water to remove residual fixative. Tissue dehydration was performed through a graded ethanol series (30-100%), with subsequent xylene clearing and paraffin embedding. Serial sections (4 μm thickness) were prepared for histological evaluation.
Tissue sections were subjected to hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and Masson's trichrome staining according to standard protocols, followed by coverslipping with mounting medium. For immunohistochemical detection, sections were incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies targeting osteocalcin (OCN; 1:100 dilution, DF12303, Affinity). Following primary antibody incubation, sections were treated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibody (room temperature, 30 minutes) and developed with diaminobenzidine substrate (10 minutes, room temperature). All stained sections were permanently mounted for microscopic evaluation.
